notes.body:
The "mission" is الدعوة — literally, the call or summons — through which the Imam of the Time reaches out to humanity. **The call is the living system of guidance** the Imam maintains in every age: a structured hierarchy of teachers and representatives who carry his knowledge, his authority, and his light into the world. Think of it like a royal dispatch network — the Imam at its center, sending out authorized messengers into every community.

A man who is "licensed" within this mission holds what is called permission (إذن) — **a delegation of spiritual authority**, not merely a certificate of learning, granted by the Imam or his senior representatives; it connects the holder to the Imam's chain of living guidance. The one who carries it is called a licensed representative (مأذون), a word rooted in the Arabic for ear, because true authorization begins with the Imam truly hearing and endorsing that person.

This is why the text treats praying in the mosque, under a مأذون, with such seriousness. The mosque led by an authorized representative of the الدعوة is not simply a building — it is **a living node in the Imam's network**, where the congregation gathers not only facing the direction of prayer (القبلة) but in spiritual alignment with the Imam's mission itself, connected to something far larger than any single act of worship.
notes.anchor: one of the licensed men of the mission leads the prayer
notes.quote: one of the licensed men of the mission leads the prayer
etymology: الدعوة (mission / the call): from root د-ع-و, to call or invite. The root yields الداعي (the caller, the representative) and the call itself. Every Arabic invitation — even a wedding دعوة — comes from here. In the Ismaili tradition, the الدعوة is Allah's standing summons to humanity, channeled through the Imam and his authorized hierarchy.

إذن (permission / authorization): from root أ-ذ-ن, meaning to give ear or to grant leave. Notice that أُذُن (the ear) shares this root — true permission begins with genuinely hearing someone. To grant إذن is to have listened and said yes. The مأذون is one whose request the Imam has truly heard and endorsed.

مأذون (the licensed representative): from root أ-ذ-ن, cast in the passive pattern مَفْعُول — meaning one to whom إذن has been given. The form signals that authority flows downward from the Imam, not upward from the crowd. He holds his role as a trust received, never self-claimed — the pattern itself encodes that humility.

notes.body:
The situation described is one where no amount of careful thinking resolves anything — the worshipper has genuinely exhausted his independent judgment (اجتهاد) and still finds both directions equally convincing. The solution is to pray twice, once facing each of the two suspected directions. One of those prayers must face the correct direction (القبلة), fulfilling the obligation regardless. The ruling is about **covering both possibilities** when the mind cannot genuinely choose between them.

The parallel ruling about four directions extends this same logic outward. If all four cardinal directions appear equally plausible — north, south, east, and west all looking like valid candidates — the worshipper prays four separate times, once toward each. When certainty is impossible, **completeness becomes the answer**.

The ruling carries mercy: the worshipper is not paralyzed by confusion, nor simply let off, but given a way forward that honors both the obligation and his genuine limitation. The tradition does not punish sincere effort — it shapes it into action.

What leads up to this ruling also matters. A worshipper who can form a judgment must form one and pray — and even if he discovers an error mid-prayer, he simply turns toward the House (الكعبة) and completes it, as long as he was not facing entirely away from it. The "pray toward both" or "pray toward all four" ruling applies only at the very **edge of total uncertainty**, when no direction prevails at all.
notes.anchor: he prays toward both directions together; and the like of this has be…
notes.quote: he prays toward both directions together; and the like of this has been mentioned concerning the four directions
etymology: القبلة (the prayer direction): from root ق-ب-ل, meaning to face, to turn toward, to receive. The verb قَبَلَ means 'he faced.' القبلة is literally 'the facing place' — the direction a worshipper turns toward Allah. The same root gives مُقَابِل (opposite, facing) and قِبَل (in front of), showing how directed orientation runs through every derivative.

اجتهاد (independent judgment): from root ج-ه-د, meaning to strive and exhaust one's effort. The verb جَهَدَ means 'he struggled.' اجتهاد is the verbal noun of the eighth verb form اِجْتَهَدَ — naming the full mental exertion applied to reach a ruling. The same root gives جِهَاد (striving) and مُجْتَهِد (one who exerts judgment): اجتهاد is the mind pushed to its absolute limit.

notes.body:
The seven ranks of prayer (صلاة) rest on **a single governing principle**: proximity to the living center of divine guidance amplifies the weight of every act of worship. Think of it like sound waves radiating from a single source — the closer you stand, the fuller and more resonant the sound.

**Each number is anchored in the spiritual arithmetic of the tradition**:

- Home → 1 prayer
- Market mosque → 12 prayers
- Tribal mosque → 25 prayers
- Congregational mosque → 100 prayers
- The Farthest Mosque → 1,000 prayers
- The Prophet's mosque in Madinah → 10,000 prayers
- The Sacred House → 100,000 prayers

Twelve is deeply embedded in Ismaili spiritual reckoning — twelve months, twelve proofs (حجج) who anchor a cycle of guidance through time. Twenty-five echoes the teaching that congregational prayer surpasses solitary prayer by that exact measure, and from a hundred onward the multiplier climbs by a factor of ten at every step, signaling not merely a larger gathering but a qualitative leap into a new order of spiritual magnitude.

The **sevenfold structure** itself carries weight. In Ismaili thought, seven marks the completed cycle: seven Imams in each prophetic era, seven degrees in the chain of divine guidance (حدود الدين), seven heavens in the cosmological map. The seven prayer-locations mirror those seven degrees exactly — at one end the solitary soul in its private room, at the other the Sacred House (الحرم), the axis around which all prayer-direction (قبلة) is oriented.

The "abundant meanings and likenesses of wisdom" that the text promises but does not supply are precisely the **inner interpretation** (تأويل) that maps each location onto a rung in the hierarchy of divine knowledge. The numbers are not prizes for religious travel; they are a map of how deeply a soul has moved toward its origin. A worshipper who grasps this does not merely count the multiplier — she or he feels the pull of that sacred center in every act of turning toward the قبلة.

etymology: مسجد (mosque): from the root س-ج-د, meaning to press the forehead to the ground in prostration. The derived noun مسجد names the place where that act of surrender (سجود) is performed. The root captures something physical — an actual pressing-down — and the word built from it carries that gravity: not just a building, but consecrated ground of bowing.

تأويل (inner interpretation): from the root أ-و-ل, meaning to return to the very first thing. The Form II verb أوّل means to lead something back to its origin, and تأويل is that act of leading back. In Ismaili thought this is exactly what inner interpretation does — it does not add new meaning to the outward text; it retrieves the first and hidden source the letter conceals.

حدود (degrees of the hierarchy): from the root ح-د-د, to sharpen or set a precise boundary. The singular حد is a sharp edge, a defined line. In Ismaili religious usage, حدود الدين are the ranked stations of the divine mission — each حد a clear boundary where one level of spiritual authority ends and the next begins.

قبلة (direction of prayer): from the root ق-ب-ل, meaning to face, to come before, or to receive. The قبلة is literally the facing — the direction toward which we turn. Crucially the root also carries the sense of reception; turning toward the قبلة is not only an act of address but an opening of oneself to what flows from that sacred center.
